title: Ring closure to tetrahydrofuran
subtitle: An intramolecular SN2: 5-exo-tet, one of the fastest ring closures

reactants.caption: 4-bromobutan-1-ol + sodium hydroxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Base and a bromoalcohol. First, make the nucleophile.
hintTiers: The neutral OH is a poor nucleophile. Which proton can hydroxide remove?
Hydroxide takes the O–H proton of the alcohol; the O–H bonding pair stays on the alcohol oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new O–H bond to the alcohol's hydrogen; the alcohol's O–H bond → lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide could displace bromide and give butane-1,4-diol, but the alkoxide formed in the flask finds its own C–Br carbon far faster: the ring closure wins.
The neutral alcohol can close the ring slowly, but the base is there to make the alkoxide, a much better nucleophile. Deprotonate first.
Hydroxide takes a proton, not the electron-rich bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: hydroxide takes the O–H proton. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

alkoxide.caption: 4-bromobutoxide + water
alkoxide.learnerPrompt: The alkoxide finds the C–Br carbon in its own chain. Close the ring.
hintTiers: An intramolecular SN2: count the ring size you would make. Which is the electrophilic carbon?
The alkoxide oxygen attacks the carbon carrying bromine, from the back; bromide leaves. A five-membered ring forms. Two arrows.
Alkoxide lone pair → new O–C bond to the CH₂ carrying bromine; that C–Br bond → lone pair on bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That takes the proton straight back from water. The alkoxide is now a good nucleophile: use it on the C–Br carbon.
That carbon has no leaving group. The electrophile is the carbon bonded to bromine.
The oxygen attacks carbon, from the side opposite bromine, not the bromine itself.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right atom: that carbon now has five bonds. Which bond breaks?

steps.explanationAfterStep: Hydroxide and the alkoxide have similar basicity, so only part of the alcohol is deprotonated at any moment. That is enough: the alkoxide closes the ring as soon as it forms.

An intramolecular SN2: 5-exo-tet in Baldwin's terms (a five-membered ring; the C–Br bond that breaks is outside the ring; the carbon attacked is tetrahedral). The chain can easily bend so the oxygen reaches the back of the C–Br bond, at 180° to it. Five-membered rings close faster than any other size except three.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide removes the O–H proton of 4-bromobutan-1-ol, and the alkoxide attacks the carbon carrying bromine in its own chain, from the back, displacing bromide: an intramolecular SN2 that gives tetrahydrofuran. In Baldwin's terms this is 5-exo-tet: a five-membered ring, the breaking bond exo (outside the new ring), at a tetrahedral carbon. Rings of five form fastest of all except three: the chain loses little freedom and the ring has almost no strain. The intermolecular SN2 with hydroxide, which would give the diol, cannot compete.
